newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany prepares to stake claim as finance centre.
newsitem.headline: Germany prepares to stake claim as finance centre.

text.p: Senior German business chiefs are due to gather in Frankfurt next Monday for the first meeting of a lobby group that wants to put Germany on the map as a key financial centre in the run-up to currency union.
The lobby group, Finanzplatz -- literally "financial centre" -- has an impressive membership register which comprises some of the leading lights of the German financial world.

Rolf Breuer, future chairman of Deutsche Bank AG and a co-founder of the group, told a news conference to announce the establishment of the group late last year: "Germany's financial centre is better than its reputation. Our aim is to have Germany join the premier league of financial centres worldwide."

The lobby group is based on a successful French initiative and aims to generate debate and push for changes to help Germany improve its standing as the 1999 launch date for the common European Economic and Monetary Union approaches.
It also aims to change the perception of the German market as an illiquid, unsophisticated market, with poor regulatory back-up, especially on insider dealing.
Finanzplatz's brief is to show that German markets are dynamic and innovative enough to withstand stiff competition from arch-rivals London and Paris.

Last week the German state secretary for the finance ministry, Juergen Stark, said that Germany plans to simplify stock market regulatory reporting rules for foreign firms and improve conditions for raising capital in hopes of wooing more firms to Germany's capital markets.
"Gaining access to capital markets has to be made easier, while investor confidence has to be boosted at the same time," Stark said.

Those seeking to sell Frankfurt as a place to do business point out that the German bond market is one of the biggest in the world, and say that the futures and options exchange (DTB) is modern and efficient with one of the best processing systems in the world.

Yet, Germany still has an image problem in many areas. A common complaint from foreign players is that German banks, including Deutsche Bank and the other two big banks -- Dresdner and Commerzbank -- have almost total control on the stock market.

However, the pro-Frankfurt lobby argues that just under half of turnover on the DTB and a third of transactions on the IBIS electronic share trading system are controlled by foreign banks, seeing this as a sign that the German market is actually far more open than many of its competitors.

Moreover it was expected that last year's Deutsche Telekom flotation, Europe's biggest ever with a planned total volume of some 20 billion marks ($13 billion), would help ease the German market's perennial problem with liquidity.

The group hopes that virtues such as these, and not least Frankfurt's future position as home to a European Central Bank, should propel the city into a prime location for issuers, investors and banks, given continued efforts to improve the range of products on offer and eliminate tax disincentives for investment here.

Yet only the most hardened patriots among the Finanzplatz lobbyists would not admit that London's capital markets have advantages in terms of personnel and experience, advantages which Frankfurt could not hope to rival.
Even the pro-Frankfurt lobby say it does not intend Frankfurt will replace London as Europe's top financial centre but rather for it to occupy a more powerful role once the Euro currency is launched.
"We cannot beat London now. But we can make sure we don't lose out to Paris," one banking source, who declined to be named, said.
